blocks.text: Ask a handful of developers what an MCP server exposes and most will say tools, maybe resources if they have read the spec closely.

Prompts get mentioned last, if at all, and that is a shame, because prompts solve a problem the other two primitives cannot touch on their own: getting a person, not the model, to kick off a well shaped task without having to compose a good prompt from scratch every single time.
This lesson opens the MCP Prompts module and lays out exactly what a prompt is, how it differs from a tool and a resource, and where it earns its keep.
1. The Prompt Primitive: A Third Kind of Capability

blocks.alt: Tools, resources, and prompts are the three MCP capabilities
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439738713-170061780.png

MCP defines three kinds of things a server can offer to a client: tools, resources, and prompts. Tools are actions the model can invoke, things like create_ticket or run_query, that have side effects or compute a result.
Resources are pieces of data the model or user can read, things like a file, a database row, or a web page. Prompts are neither.
A prompt is a reusable instruction template, something a person selects on purpose, fills in with a few concrete details, and sends off as a ready made request.

The distinction matters because each primitive answers a different question. A tool answers do this. A resource answers read this. A prompt answers here is a good way to ask for something you probably want to ask for often.

Where tools and resources are largely aimed at what the model can reach for during its own reasoning, prompts are aimed squarely at the human sitting in front of the client, giving that person a shortcut to a well phrased request instead of a blank text box.

It helps to notice that all three primitives are declared up front during the capabilities exchange when a client connects to a server, so a host knows immediately, before any conversation happens, whether the server it just connected to offers any prompts at all, and if so, how many, without needing to guess or probe for them.
2. Prompts Are Not Tools, and They Are Not Resources

blocks.alt: A prompt is compared against a tool and against a resource
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439738714-123517993.png

It helps to be precise about the boundary. A tool call happens because the model decided, mid reasoning, that it needed to take an action or fetch a fact. A prompt is invoked because a user, browsing a menu of available templates, picked one on purpose before any model reasoning about the task even began. The model is downstream of a prompt selection, not the one making it.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Primitive","Who triggers it","What it produces","Typical shape"],"rows":[["Tool","The model, during reasoning","A side effect or a computed result","A function call with typed arguments"],["Resource","The model or the user","Raw content to read","A URI resolving to text, JSON, or binary data"],["Prompt","The user, before reasoning starts","A ready made message or message sequence","A named template with argument placeholders"]]}

blocks.text: Keeping these three separate in your head pays off the moment you start designing a server. If you catch yourself building a prompt that actually performs an action, like sending an email as a side effect of being invoked, you have drifted into tool territory and should probably expose a tool instead. Prompts exist to produce a message, nothing more.
2.1 The Same Task, Three Different Shapes
Suppose a user wants the current weather for a city. As a tool, the model calls get_weather with a city argument because it decided, mid reasoning, that it needed that fact.
As a resource, the client reads weather://city/tokyo because something, model or user, wants to look at that data directly.

As a prompt, a user might invoke a weather_report prompt that asks the model to produce a nicely worded, multi paragraph forecast summary rather than just the raw numbers, a job specifically about phrasing, not about fetching the number itself.

items: Tool call: get_weather(city=Tokyo), model decided to fetch a fact mid reasoning
Resource read: weather://city/tokyo, raw data handed over as is
Prompt: weather_report(city=Tokyo), a user asked for a nicely phrased forecast writeup

blocks.text: 3. Why Prompts Exist: The User Intent Problem

Plenty of tasks people bring to an AI assistant are not one off curiosities, they are things the same person, or every person on a team, does over and over: write a bug report from a stack trace, summarize a long document before a meeting, translate a paragraph into another language.
Each of these has a shape, a set of things you need to fill in, and a decent structure for the result.
Without prompts, every user reinvents that structure by typing it out freehand, and the quality of the outcome depends entirely on how good their freehand prompt happened to be that day.

A prompt template captures the good version once, at the server author's leisure, and hands it to every user forever after. Instead of typing paragraphs of instructions about tone, structure, and required fields, a user picks Draft Bug Report from a list, fills in three short fields, and gets the same well engineered request that an expert prompt writer would have typed by hand.
4. Who Chooses a Prompt: The User, Not the Model

blocks.alt: A user chooses a prompt rather than the model deciding
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439738714-184793247.png
This is worth repeating because it trips people up: prompt selection is a user action, surfaced through the host application, not something the model autonomously decides to do mid conversation.
A host might show prompts as a slash command menu, a dropdown, or a quick action button.

The user clicks or types their way to a specific named prompt, the host asks the server to fill in the template with whatever arguments the user supplied, and only then does the resulting message enter the conversation with the model.

Some hosts do let a model suggest a relevant prompt to the user, as a kind of hint, but suggesting is different from invoking. The actual decision to run a specific prompt template with specific argument values is a user level action, which is precisely why prompts are documented as user controlled in the protocol, in contrast to tools, which are model controlled.
5. Anatomy at a Glance: Name, Description, Arguments

Every prompt a server exposes has three basic parts: a short machine friendly name, a human readable description explaining what it does, and a list of arguments it accepts, each with its own name and description. This lesson only needs the shape for now, the next lesson in this module goes much deeper into how each part is defined and used.

A client that wants to show this prompt to a user already has everything it needs from that shape alone: a title to display, a sentence explaining what it does, and a small form asking for document_text and, optionally, max_points.

Each of those three parts answers a distinct question a client needs answered before it can even show the prompt to a user. The name answers what do I call this when I ask for it. The description answers what should I tell the user this does. The argument list answers what form fields do I need to render, and which of them can the user leave blank.
6. From Template to Message: The Filling Step

blocks.alt: A template is filled with arguments to produce a message
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439738714-501167618.png

A prompt template is only half the story, the other half is what happens when a user supplies values for its arguments. The client sends a prompts get request naming the prompt and the argument values, the server fills the template with those values, and returns one or more ready made messages, already phrased and structured, that the host can hand straight to the model.

code.content:
import mcp_client

result = await mcp_client.get_prompt(
    name="summarize_document",
    arguments={"document_text": long_text, "max_points": "5"},
)
for message in result.messages:
    print(message.role, ":", message.content.text)

blocks.text: Notice that the client never has to know how the template is written, whether it is a plain string with substitutions or something more elaborate. It only ever deals with a name, some argument values going in, and a list of finished messages coming out. That clean boundary is what makes prompts portable across very different servers and very different client implementations.
7. Example Use Case: Drafting a Bug Report
Picture a developer who just hit a crash and has a raw stack trace sitting in their clipboard.

Instead of writing a paragraph explaining what a good bug report should contain, they invoke a draft_bug_report prompt, paste the stack trace and a one line description of what they were doing, and the server returns a fully structured message asking the model to produce a title, a reproduction summary, the likely root cause, and a suggested fix, all in the house format their team's issue tracker expects.

The value here is not that the model could not have written a bug report without help, it is that every developer on the team now produces bug reports with the same structure, the same level of detail, and the same missing fields caught, because the template enforces it every single time it is used.
8. Example Use Case: Summarizing a Document

A summarize_document prompt takes a long piece of text and an optional length preference, and returns a message asking the model for a summary in a specific style, perhaps bullet points capped at a chosen count, perhaps a short paragraph for an executive audience. Different callers can supply different arguments while relying on the same underlying instructions for tone, structure, and what to leave out.

This is a good example of a prompt that benefits from optional arguments. A sensible default length applies when max_points is omitted, but a user who explicitly wants three points instead of the usual five can say so without needing a different prompt entirely.
9. Example Use Case: Translating Text

A translate_text prompt accepts the source text and a target language, and returns a message instructing the model to translate faithfully, preserve formatting, and flag anything ambiguous rather than guessing silently. Because the instructions about tone, faithfulness, and how to handle ambiguity live in the template rather than in each user's head, translations produced this way are far more consistent than ones produced from ad hoc, freely typed requests.
10. Prompts as Structured Shortcuts to Good Prompting

Underneath all three examples is the same idea: a prompt is a way of packaging expertise about how to ask for something well, so that the person asking does not need that expertise themselves. The server author, who understands what makes a good bug report or a good summary, writes that understanding into the template once. Every user of the prompt benefits from it without having to learn it.

blocks.title: A useful mental model
blocks.content: Think of a prompt template the way you would think of a well designed form at a government office. You do not need to know the legal language the form eventually produces, you just fill in the blanks it asks for, and the form itself guarantees the output has everything it needs.

blocks.text: 11. How the Client and Host Surface Prompts to Users

A host application typically lists the prompts a connected server offers as a menu, often triggered by a slash command or an explicit prompts button in the interface. When a user selects one, the host renders a small form based on the prompt's declared arguments, required fields marked clearly, optional ones left blank by default, then sends the filled values back to the server through the client's prompts get call.

None of this rendering logic is specified down to the pixel by MCP itself, different hosts are free to present prompts however suits their interface, a command palette, a dropdown, a chat style form. What is fixed is the underlying protocol contract: a list of named prompts with described arguments, and a way to request a filled result for a chosen set of argument values.

A useful comparison is a text editor's command palette. You do not need to know how a command is implemented to use it, you type a few letters, see a short description, and press enter. A prompt menu works the same way for the user: they see a name and a description, not the underlying template text, and the mechanics of filling it in happen entirely behind that simple interaction.
12. Prompts Can Pull In Live Resource Content Too

A particularly powerful pattern, covered in full in a later lesson in this module called Context Injection, is a prompt template that does not just take user typed arguments, it also reaches out and reads a resource on the server's own side while filling itself in.

A code review prompt might accept a file path argument and then have the server actually read that file's current contents as a resource, embedding the real code directly into the filled message rather than asking the user to paste it by hand.

This is one of the reasons prompts and resources are designed to compose so naturally: a prompt template is free to reference resource URIs internally, turning a short user provided argument into a much richer, fully populated message.
13. Prompts Are Server Owned, Not Client Owned

blocks.alt: A prompt is owned by the server rather than the client
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439738715-286431301.png

A prompt template lives entirely on the server side. The client and host never see or store the actual instruction text that makes up the template, they only see its name, description, and argument list until the moment they ask the server to fill it in.

This matters for the same reason resource and tool definitions living on the server matters: the server author can improve the wording of a template, fix a bug in its instructions, or add a new optional argument, and every client automatically benefits the next time it asks, with zero changes needed on the client side.

items: The server defines what prompts exist and what their template text says
The client only ever sees names, descriptions, and argument metadata until it asks for a filled result
Improving a template on the server benefits every connected client immediately

blocks.text: 14. The Result of a Prompt Is Messages, Not Just a String

blocks.alt: A filled prompt returns a list of messages rather than a plain string
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439738715-127230872.png
It is tempting to think of a filled prompt as a single string of text, but the protocol actually returns a list of messages, each with a role, typically user or assistant, and content.

This lets a single prompt template seed an entire mini conversation rather than a single line, for example a template that returns one user message containing the request and one assistant message containing a worked example of the expected output format, priming the model with a demonstration before it even starts on the real task.

Most simple prompts return just one user message, but the option to return several is what allows more elaborate templates, including ones that embed a short example exchange, to exist within the exact same mechanism.
14.1 Why Bother With Multiple Messages

Returning more than one message lets a template do a bit of light teaching before the real request. A code review prompt, for instance, might return one assistant message showing a short example review of a trivial snippet, then a user message with the actual code to review, so the model has a concrete demonstration of the expected tone and level of detail before it tackles the real file.
15. Prompts vs Tools vs Resources: When to Reach for Each

blocks.alt: Wanting a user triggered template points toward a prompt
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439738926-659590692.png

A practical rule of thumb: if the model needs to decide, mid task, to fetch a fact or take an action, that is a tool or a resource. If a human wants a fast, well phrased way to kick off a recurring kind of request, that is a prompt. The three are not competitors, a well designed server usually offers all three, tools for actions the model takes autonomously, resources for data either side can read, and prompts for the handful of common requests a human wants a shortcut to.

blocks.text: 16. What Prompts Are Not Good For
Prompts are not a substitute for tools when an actual action needs to happen, and they are not a substitute for resources when the goal is simply handing over raw data.
A prompt that tries to both fill in a nice message and quietly perform a side effect, like sending an email, is mixing responsibilities that the protocol deliberately keeps apart.
If you find a template growing an action inside it, that is a signal to split the action out into a tool and keep the prompt focused purely on producing a good message.

Prompts are also a poor fit for fully open ended requests that never repeat. If a user's request is genuinely one of a kind, with no recurring shape, a plain typed message to the model is simpler and more honest than forcing it through a rigid template with placeholders that do not quite fit.
17. Prompts Inside a Larger Conversation

A filled prompt rarely stands alone forever, once its messages enter the conversation, the model can respond, the user can follow up, and the exchange continues like any other conversation from that point on. The prompt's job ends the moment its messages are handed over, it does not keep controlling the conversation afterward, and the user is free to steer things in a completely different direction on the very next turn.

This is an important boundary to hold onto: a prompt seeds a conversation, it does not own it. Once the filled messages are appended to the transcript, ordinary conversational turns take over exactly as if the user had typed those messages by hand.
18. A Family of Related Prompts

Server authors often expose several prompts that are variations on a theme rather than one giant, overloaded template. A documentation server might offer explain_concept, summarize_page, and generate_faq as three separate, focused prompts instead of one explain_or_summarize_or_generate_faq prompt with a mode argument, because separate names are easier for a user to browse, easier to describe accurately, and easier to keep simple internally.

items: explain_concept: takes a topic name, returns a plain language explanation
summarize_page: takes a page's text, returns a short summary
generate_faq: takes a page's text, returns a list of likely questions and answers

blocks.text: A consistent naming convention across a family of prompts, verb first and specific, makes a server's entire prompt menu easier to scan and choose from at a glance, which matters more than it sounds like it should once a server offers a dozen or more of them.
Worked Example
A small internal tool team runs an MCP server for their support desk. They expose a triage_ticket prompt with two arguments, customer_message, required, and priority_hint, optional.
A support agent pastes in a customer's raw message, leaves priority_hint blank because they are not sure yet, and invokes the prompt.
The server fills the template, asking the model to classify the ticket's likely category, suggest a priority level, and draft a first reply, and returns that as a single, ready to send user message.

code.content:
filled = await client.get_prompt(
    name="triage_ticket",
    arguments={"customer_message": raw_message},
)
draft_message = filled.messages[0].content.text
send_to_model(draft_message)

blocks.text: The agent never had to remember what fields a good triage request needs, the template already encoded that. Every ticket triaged this way, by any agent on the team, gets the same consistent structure and the same quality bar, which is exactly the payoff a good prompt template is meant to deliver.
The team also defines the prompt's argument shape in a small table so every agent on the team can see, at a glance, exactly what triage_ticket expects.

blocks.text: Common Mistakes

items: Confusing a prompt with a tool and having it silently perform a side effect, like sending a message, instead of only producing text
Assuming the model chooses which prompt to run, when in fact prompt selection is a user driven action surfaced by the host
Building a prompt that requires the user to type in content the server could have fetched itself as a resource
Treating the filled result as a single string rather than a list of role tagged messages, and mishandling multi message templates
Writing a prompt so specific to one narrow scenario that it is really a one off, not a genuinely reusable template
Forgetting that the template text itself lives only on the server, and trying to inspect or cache it client side instead of asking fresh

blocks.text: Practice

Design a prompt definition, as a JSON object with name, description, and arguments, for a request you personally make often, something like drafting a meeting agenda from a list of topics, or writing a commit message from a diff summary. Decide which arguments are required and which are optional, then write out, in plain English, what the filled message should look like for one concrete set of argument values.
Key Takeaway

A prompt is a reusable, server owned instruction template, chosen deliberately by a user rather than triggered by model reasoning, that gets filled with concrete argument values and returned as one or more ready made messages. It stands apart from tools, which perform actions, and resources, which expose raw data, by focusing purely on packaging good, repeatable requests, whether that is drafting a bug report, summarizing a document, or translating text.

With the concept of a prompt clear, the next lesson in this module, Prompt Templates, zooms into the anatomy of a template itself: exactly how a name, a description, and argument placeholders are declared, and the mechanics of how concrete values get substituted in to produce the final message.
